old.the_universe_expanded_faster_than_the_: The universe expanded faster than the speed of light by a factor of ~10²⁶. Smoothed out the early universe. Solves the "horizon problem" (why opposite sides of the sky have the same temperature). Quantum fluctuations during inflation became the seeds of all later structure.
old.the_big_bang_theory_describes_the_univ: The Big Bang theory describes the universe from about 1 second after t=0 onward. What about the first second — or rather, the first 10⁻³⁰ of a second? That is where cosmic inflation lives, and where modern cosmology meets quantum field theory, string theory, and the genuinely open question of whether other universes exist.
old.alan_guth_then_a_young_postdoc_at_corn: Alan Guth (then a young postdoc working on the monopole problem, at Cornell and then SLAC) realized that if the very early universe went through a brief period of exponential expansion — doubling in size many dozens of times in a tiny fraction of a second — all three problems could be solved at once. The horizon problem: regions that look causally separated NOW were once in tiny causal contact BEFORE inflation, then stretched far apart. The flatness problem: exponential expansion smooths out any curvature, the way blowing up a balloon makes its surface look locally flat. The monopole problem: if monopoles formed before inflation, they got diluted to undetectable density. The brief moment of inflation needs to last from about 10⁻³⁶ to 10⁻³² seconds after t=0, expanding space by a factor of at least e^60 (~10²⁶).
old.inflation_predicts_specific_signatures: Inflation predicts specific signatures in the CMB. (1) Nearly scale-invariant primordial fluctuations: the same statistical pattern across all length scales. Planck measured the spectral index n_s = 0.965 ± 0.004, slightly less than 1, exactly as slow-roll inflation predicts (a perfectly scale-invariant spectrum would be 1.000). (2) Gaussian statistics: fluctuations follow a normal distribution. Observed. (3) A small amount of spatial curvature consistent with zero (flatness). Observed. (4) Adiabatic perturbations: matter + photons fluctuate together, not independently. Observed. (5) Tensor modes (primordial gravitational waves) — NOT yet observed, but their non-detection constrains many inflation models.
old.we_cannot_directly_observe_inflation_i: We cannot directly observe inflation itself; we observe its predicted CMB signatures. We cannot communicate with or measure other "bubble" universes, by construction (faster-than-light expansion separates them). We cannot test what happened BEFORE the Planck time (~10⁻⁴³ s), when known physics breaks down. We cannot derive the values of the constants from first principles in any known theory — we can only measure them. These are not gaps inflation needs to fix; they are limits on what physics can know at present. Quantum gravity, when it arrives, may move these limits. Or it may simply reveal new limits underneath.

new.the_universe_expanded_faster_than_the_: A proposed early phase of accelerated expansion. In nearly exponential models, physical separations grow rapidly while the comoving Hubble length shrinks. This can stretch initially small perturbations to large scales. The timing, amount of expansion and transition to the hot phase depend on the model.
new.the_big_bang_theory_describes_the_univ: The hot Big Bang describes an early hot, dense phase of the universe and its later expansion and cooling. Inflation is a proposed earlier stage of accelerated expansion. Its dynamics, how it ended, and how its energy became a hot plasma are active questions. Other universes require additional assumptions beyond the measured CMB statistics.
new.alan_guth_then_a_young_postdoc_at_corn: Guth proposed a period of accelerated expansion to address the horizon, flatness and monopole puzzles. For nearly constant expansion rate H, the scale factor grows approximately as exp(Ht). A region that was causally connected beforehand can become much larger; sufficient expansion reduces the relative effect of spatial curvature and dilutes relics such as hypothetical monopoles. Sixty e-folds is a common illustration, not a universally measured duration. The required expansion and its timing depend on the inflation model and the later thermal history.
new.inflation_predicts_specific_signatures: CMB measurements support nearly Gaussian, largely adiabatic primordial perturbations with a spectrum close to scale invariance. Planck 2018 temperature, polarization and lensing results infer nₛ = 0.9649 ± 0.0042 at 68% confidence. This agrees with many slow-roll models and constrains others; it does not identify a unique inflation mechanism. BICEP/Keck XIII (2021) reports the tensor-to-scalar ratio r < 0.036 at 95% confidence using observations through 2018 with Planck and WMAP. That result is an upper limit, not a detection of primordial tensors.
new.we_cannot_directly_observe_inflation_i: The observations shown here constrain primordial statistics through a cosmological analysis. They do not directly measure the chosen pattern, amount of expansion or duration in this explorer. Different inflation models can give similar spectra while differing in their potentials and reheating histories. Claims about eternal inflation or other universes add assumptions that these measurements do not establish. Where classical gravity breaks down, a quantum description of gravity would be needed.

caveats.old: caveat: 'Guth\'s original model had a problem: it couldn\'t end gracefully. Andrei Linde + Andreas Albrecht + Paul Steinhardt (independently, 1982) proposed "new inflation" and then "slow-roll inflation" that fixed this. The family of working models is now large, which is part of inflation\'s critique: it can fit almost anything.'
caveats.new: caveat: 'Guth’s original false-vacuum model could not complete the transition to a hot universe successfully. Later proposals changed the dynamics. A viable model must specify how inflation ends, account for reheating, and satisfy observational constraints.'

caveats.old: caveat: 'BICEP2 announced detection of primordial gravitational waves in 2014 → would have been Nobel-level evidence for inflation. Within a year, the signal turned out to be Milky Way dust, not cosmological. CMB-S4 (proposed) and LiteBIRD (Japan, 2032 launch) aim to make the definitive measurement. If primordial B-modes are detected, inflation goes from "favored theory" to "confirmed."'
caveats.new: caveat: 'Galactic dust and gravitational lensing also produce B-mode polarization. A primordial tensor claim requires careful foreground removal and consistency checks. Such a result would test early-universe mechanisms; it would not automatically establish a unique inflaton model or a multiverse.'

caveats.old: caveat: 'In every era of physics, some questions seemed permanently unanswerable until they weren\'t. Some never moved at all. We do not know in advance which category a question is in. The honest answer to "did inflation really happen?" is: probably, mostly, in some form. The honest answer to "are there other universes?" is: we genuinely don\'t know, and may never know.'
caveats.new: caveat: 'Distinguish mathematical predictions, observational inference and additional assumptions. CMB statistics can test early-universe models. Eternal inflation and other-universe proposals require further assumptions and face open problems of observation.'
